Adult Emus (Dromaius novaehollandiae) are the second-largest living birds by height, with individuals commonly attaining a 134 centimeter [Li = 134 centimeter] total body length from beak tip to tail, a measurement that far exceeds that of most extant ratites except the ostrich. This elongated stature is accompanied by a substantial body mass; fully grown birds typically reach an ultimate wet weight of 55000 grams [Wwi = 55000 grams], placing them among the heaviest of the paleognathous avifauna. The metabolic demands of sustaining such a large body are considerable, and reproductive output is correspondingly modulated. Under controlled captive conditions at a core body temperature of 37.98 °C [T = 37.98 °C], female Emus in peak breeding condition produce, on average, between 6 and 8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 6 and 8 eggs per clutch] and may lay up to 3 such clutches across a single breeding season [F_R_i = up to 3 such clutches across a single breeding season], resulting in an annual egg production of approximately 10 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 10 eggs per year].

During the initial phase of life, the newly hatched chick, or precocial downy young, weighs approximately 420 grams [Wwb = approximately 420 grams], a comparatively large birth mass that reflects the considerable yolk reserves packaged within the egg and provides a competitive advantage in the harsh, resource-scarce environments typical of the Australian outback. This substantial neonatal mass supports the chick's rapid development during the first days post-hatching. Incubation of the large, dark-green eggs occurs at a mean temperature of 35.95 °C [T = 35.95 °C], a thermal regime that results in an average incubation period of 53 days [ab = 53 days], which is among the lengthiest incubation durations recorded for any bird species. The incubation duties are performed exclusively by the male parent, who fasts for the entire period, losing a significant proportion of his body mass. Upon emergence, the chick is striped and capable of independent locomotion, feeding itself on insects and plant matter from its first day, a precocial strategy that contrasts sharply with the altricial development seen in many passerines.

Following the energetically demanding incubation, the male parent provides no further direct provisioning, yet the chick must undergo a series of critical developmental transitions. Under typical thermal conditions with an ambient temperature approximating 37.98 °C [T = 37.98 °C] during active foraging periods, the young Emu reaches the fledging milestone at just 4.5 days after hatching [tx = 4.5 days after hatching]. This remarkably early fledging interval reflects the rapid maturation of leg and foot coordination necessary for terrestrial escape from predators, rather than the development of flight feathers, which are vestigial in ratites. However, the juvenile then enters a protracted sub-adult phase. Growth is steady but gradual, and the end of the immature juvenile period, marking the onset of puberty, is not reached until approximately 457.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 457.5 days after hatching], a developmental delay that allows for the full acquisition of adult skeletal and muscular mass needed for future soci at a temperature of 37.98 °C [T = 37.98 °C]al competition.

The timeline to actual first breeding is even more prolonged than the pubertal transition, reflecting the significant time required to establish a territory and secure a mate in a polyandrous system. Field records indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 912 days [tR = 912 days], which is equivalent to roughly two and a half years, when measured at the typical active core temperature of 37.98 °C [T = 37.98 °C]. This deferred onset of reproductive effort contrasts with smaller ratites but is consistent with the slow maturation observed in large-bodied avian herbivores. Males typically commence nesting at this age, constructing a shallow scrape on the ground that holds the clutch of several eggs laid by multiple females in succession. This breeding system, where females may mate with several males, places a premium on male parental investment, as the male alone will incubate the eggs and guard the precocial chicks for an extended period following hatching.

Long-term mark-recapture studies of wild populations, alongside captive colony records, have documented the maximum lifespan of Dromaius novaehollandiae to be 14600 days [am = 14600 days], which is approximately 40 years [am = approximately 40 years] under optimal conditions, measured at the species' characteristic core body temperature of 37.98 °C [T = 37.98 °C]. This exceptional longevity is among the highest recorded for any terrestrial bird of equivalent mass, rivalling that of the larger ostrich. Such an extended lifespan is a hallmark of a slow life-history strategy, characterized by deferred reproduction, large offspring size, and protracted parental care exclusively provided by the male. Encounters with senescent adults in the wild, identified by worn plumage, reduced locomotive speed, and diminished reproductive output, provide further insight into the natural mortality and post-reproductive senescence that ultimately conclude the species' life cycle, underscoring the evolutionary trade-offs inherent in its ecological niche as a large, desert-adapted omnivore.
